w: What's tested Why we mount casts: diagnosis (CR vs MIP mountings), treatment planning, diagnostic waxing, treatment Arcon vs non-arcon; the UAB classification (non-adjustable, semi-adjustable, fully adjustable) Non-adjustable articulators: accurate in one position only, who benefits, mounting without a facebow Semi-adjustable: sagittal condylar inclination and the Bennett angle; the facebow, CR record, MIP record and eccentric records, and the errors each one prevents or causes Fully adjustable: kinematic facebow, pantograph, why record thickness doesn't matter there but does on a semi-adjustable Choosing an articulator: the patient's occlusion, the extent of the work, the instrument's limits, the clinician Dr. Givan opened the second half of the course (10/22) with the devices we use to relate the arches. "It seems every concept of occlusal therapy developed an articulator": many of the old concepts were driven by what a machine could do. Today it is much simpler, and he sorts everything into three groups: you can't adjust it, you can adjust some of it, or you program all of it. The equipment is only a tool; the goal is to treat the patient. His one line to remember: an articulator has its best value when it is similar in size to the patient. What we use articulators for Diagnosis. Mounted diagnostic casts improve visualization of the static and functional relationships of the teeth and make it easier to replicate mandibular movement and the contacts it produces. Pathologic contacts often can't be seen clinically, because protective neuromuscular reflexes steer the patient around them, but properly mounted casts show them. A CR mounting is the most useful for diagnosis: it allows the fullest range of movement, so you can evaluate every contact and slide, close into CO (often unstable) and still move into MIP. An MIP mounting can't reposition the condyles to CR, so it can't show the CO contacts. From a CR mounting you can always find MIP; from an MIP mounting you can't get back to CO. Treatment planning. Mounted casts help build a sequential plan that removes the causes of disease and restores function and esthetics: you can visualize each step on the articulator first, for example a selective grinding (equilibration). Diagnostic waxing develops the tooth forms in wax to see the final goal and the problems that may come up, and to plan spacing, orthodontics, hard and soft tissue grafting, the occlusion, fixed and removable tooth-, implant- and tissue-supported prostheses, and esthetics. It is also used to address the patient's expectations: a patient who doesn't understand dentistry understands a cast in front of them. Treatment. The most common use of an articulator is treatment: some materials and methods for making a prosthesis aren't appropriate for the mouth (indirect fabrication), and moving the articulator helps build it. "If I could get one point across today": your choice of articulator will make or break your time treating the patient. Anything you can do outside an appointment to make the appointment faster is money well spent; an articulator that replicates the patient makes crown and denture deliveries go much faster. Classifying articulators Arcon stands for ARticulating CONdyle: the condylar element is on the lower member of the articulator and the fossa element on the upper member, as in the patient. A non-arcon articulator has them the other way around; it is often cheaper, but, for example, you can't change the vertical dimension as easily without throwing off your records. The UAB accepted classification has three groups. Non-adjustable: hinge and average-value articulators (not programmable). Semi-adjustable: some settings, some averages (for example the Denar 320, the one you have). Fully adjustable: everything is programmed. Articulators don't fit neatly into these groups: it's a continuum, and some semi-adjustable articulators are nearly fully adjustable. Virtual articulators in digital dentistry are "not quite yet, but close." Software can replicate a mechanical articulator's shape and motion, and digital work can combine intraoral scans, CBCT data and facial and esthetic landmarks. What they still lack is accurately positioning the models to the patient, the equivalent of a facebow (a digital facebow that puts the maxillary teeth in the same 3-D relation to the joints). Digital is pushing dentistry back toward fully adjustable articulation, which the mechanical world had drifted away from because it was so hard to do. Non-adjustable articulators No adjustment can bring a non-adjustable articulator closer to the patient. Its movements range from a hinge only to eccentric movements based on averages. However different they look (a palm-sized hinge, one glued to the back of the cast, one that looks like yours with no adjustments), they are all accurate in only one contact position, MICP. Their opening and closing paths and all their eccentric motions don't reflect the patient. The procedure is an arbitrary mounting in MICP. Any interocclusal record that separates the teeth increases the error, because when it is removed the articulator closes along a different arc from the patient's mandible. The smaller the articulator compared with the patient, the larger that error. Advantages: low expense and little effort. But that benefits the lab, not the dentist: labs like these because they are quick, inexpensive and small (low shipping costs), and dentists often don't ask for more ("all you have to do is ask"). Because the articulator doesn't replicate the patient, the restoration can't meet the occlusal requirements of the patient's eccentric movements, so the dentist spends chair time adjusting it, and grinding often destroys anatomic contour and leaves poor occlusal relationships (zirconia, which doesn't adjust or polish well, makes this worse). Partial-arch articulators also can't verify the mounting cross-arch or let you model the occlusal form from the opposite side. "There is never an advantage to the dentist for the lab to use this articulator": its hinge axis can be very different from the anatomic one, sometimes directly behind the second molar, and it can't move in pathways like the patient's. Dentists seem to accept that adjusting crowns is normal: "NO!" The exception: a non-adjustable articulator about the size of a person, with the condyles roughly 4 inches apart and the maxillary cast placed in about the right orientation to them (for example the Hanau-Mate from Whip Mix), builds crowns that roughly match the patient's movement. Mounting without a facebow. Use an articulator with an intercondylar distance of about 110 mm (4 inches) and a universal mounting stand. Secure the stand's platform to the lower member; center the maxillary cast on its positioning lines; fix it with utility wax, sticky wax or hot glue; attach it to the upper member's mounting plate with stone or plaster; when that has set, remove the platform; relate the mandibular cast with a bite registration if needed; with the articulator inverted, attach the lower cast to the lower mounting plate; when that has set, turn it upright and remove the registration. The casts are now in the Bonwill position, where the average protrusive angle (condylar inclination), immediate side shift (Bennett movement) and progressive side shift can be used without patient records. Semi-adjustable articulators Some settings let a semi-adjustable articulator resemble the patient more closely (how many depends on the model), so occlusal contacts and eccentric motions can be replicated to nearly match the patient. One semi-adjustable articulator can be used for almost anything, from a single crown to a full-mouth reconstruction with a change in vertical dimension, if you know how to use it. Why would you ever restore anterior teeth on a non-adjustable articulator when a semi-adjustable one moves in the right direction? The two common adjustments: 1. Sagittal condylar inclination (SCI), also called condylar guidance: the angle at which the condyle descends the articular eminence in the sagittal plane. It controls the disclusion of the posterior teeth when there is little or no anterior guidance, and it affects cusp height and fossa depth. It can be customized to the patient's eminence (one protrusive record sets both sides) or set arbitrarily: 20-30° is common for fixed work, and about 0° for neutrocentric dentures. Matching the patient's protrusive function is especially helpful for bilateral balanced occlusion in dentures. (Desired touching is a "contact"; undesired touching is an "interference".) 2. Bennett angle: in mediotrusion the orbiting condyle moves inward (anterior, inferior and medial), which affects the width of the central fossae of the posterior teeth. It is the angle of that inward path in the horizontal plane relative to a straight protrusive path, set on the medial wall of the fossa. More sophisticated instruments can also set the immediate lateral mandibular translation (immediate side shift, ISS). The Bennett angle is less commonly adjusted: "if I was going to leave any feature off of an articulator, I'd probably leave this one," because the average values are close enough for most general dentistry. Because the articulator can be adjusted, information must be gathered from the patient: 1. a facebow transfer (mounts the maxillary cast), 2. a centric relation record and 3. eccentric records (MIP, lateral, protrusive), which mount the mandibular cast and program the articulator. The goal is opening and closing paths as close as possible to the patient's, to minimize interferences. The facebow transfer The facebow mounts the maxillary cast (never the mandibular) in a similar relation to the patient's hinge axis, for function and esthetics. It consists of an ear-bow (caliper), a transfer assembly and a bite plate, and it needs a reference plane defined by three points on the patient that are calibrated to the articulator: two posterior points, usually the auditory canals, which estimate the transverse horizontal hinge axis, and one anterior point, which depends on the system (nasion, orbitale, or a set distance from the edge of the maxillary teeth). The reference plane is usually the Frankfort horizontal (some use Camper's plane). In an indirect mounting only the transfer assembly is attached to the lower member of the articulator to mount the cast, which simplifies mounting and lets the ear-bow stay in the clinic. Facebows for semi-adjustable articulators don't try to locate the exact hinge axis: they estimate an arbitrary posterior point near it, typically within 2-5 mm, much more accurate than a mounting stand. The auditory canals are the clinical reference, but the bow is designed with an arbitrary hinge axis in front of the ears. That is an arbitrary facebow; a bow that locates the exact hinge axis is a kinematic facebow. "99.9% of patients" are treated well with an arbitrary facebow; the small error is clinically insignificant. The school's clinical guideline for the Denar Slidematic facebow (about 1.5 minutes; in class he said 30-50 seconds): the anterior reference point is 43 mm above the right lateral incisal edge (#7), marked with a ruler (adjacent teeth or the lower border of the upper lip at rest if #7 is missing); PVS on the bite plate captures the cusp tips and incisal edges, held with cotton rolls; the transfer assembly goes on the ear-bow, then into the ear canals; the pointer is aimed at the mark, the bow is checked level (its horizontal level parallels the bench top) and in the facial midline, the clamps are tightened, and the transfer jig goes to the mounting table. The level is what captures the esthetic planes: a cant of the incisal plane and the tilt of the occlusal plane come to the articulator, where you can see them. Without a facebow the instrument loses much of its value. Incorrect maxillary orientation gives an error in the esthetic plane (risk of an occlusal cant: you hesitate to hand the patient the mirror), an error in the occlusal plane (risk of protrusive, non-working and working interferences), possibly incorrect cusp height, and grooves and cusps that don't match the patient. The result is more chairside adjustment, often ablating anatomic form: more work for the dentist to fix, if possible, what was easily avoided. Hinge axis and facebow. The facebow relates the maxilla to both the patient's hinge axis (PHA) and the articulator's hinge axis (AHA). With a kinematic facebow, AHA = PHA; with an arbitrary facebow, AHA is near PHA. Mounting errors show up in protrusion and laterotrusion: a cast mounted too posterior or too superior gives premature or heavy contacts on the most anterior teeth; too anterior or too inferior gives premature or heavy contacts on the most posterior teeth. The centric relation record CO is often unstable, so an interocclusal record is needed to mount in CR, and from a CR mounting you can easily move to MICP. It is most appropriate for diagnosis, for reorganized dentistry and for changes in VDO. Wax is often preferred: an immediate set (soften it, hit it with the air-water syringe), minimal trimming, repeatable for verification, and because it doesn't capture fine anatomy, the opposing cusp tips seat into it "like clockwork". It is fragile. Some techniques use VPS (the Lucia jig, the leaf gauge). The record is made without tooth contact, because contact triggers the neuromuscular reflexes that deviate the jaw toward MIP, and at the smallest opening that avoids tooth contact: the more the vertical is opened, the larger the error, because an arbitrary axis is being used. Or make it at the vertical dimension you intend to restore. Stability of CO. When MIP = CO, the contacts are stable and distributed and the vertical is stable: the ideal mounted relationship for reorganized treatment (dentures, full-mouth rehabilitation, full-arch implant work). But MIP ≠ CO in about 90% of people. Closing with the joints seated, neuromuscular control may not bring the jaw to MIP (sleep, rapid closure), and the resulting interferences lead to wear facets, tooth and cusp fracture, mobility and pain. The closure from CO to MIP decreases the VDO, positions the mandible anteriorly and has many potential interferences. So the CR mounting matters most for diagnosis, while treatment is usually conformative. The MIP record Mounting in MIP (also called MICP or ICP) is simpler than a CR mounting, because MICP is often more stable than CO, and it is the most appropriate for conformative restorative dentistry. Its significant limitation: the casts can't move posteriorly-superiorly to show any slide from CO to MICP, and since the start isn't joint-seated, eccentric motion is inaccurate unless it is tooth guided. It is the most common record and "also the most misused record." The number one cause of lab problems is a bad impression; the second is the mounting, usually from misusing MIP records. The most important rule: hand-articulate the casts whenever you can, and use a registration only if they are unstable. If you send the lab a record, they will mount with it, so don't send one "just in case." VPS (vinyl polysiloxane, polyvinyl siloxane) is the common material, but it must be trimmed to seat accurately, and its resilience is a problem without adequate posterior stops. Its working time is 30-60 seconds minimum from the start of the mix at 72°F (22°C) and its minimum removal time 1 minute 30 seconds: hard to hold still, and a patient who moves as it sets distorts it invisibly. It is also hard to reseat clinically to confirm the registration. Waxes are generally easier and highly accurate: aluminous wax (Aluwax) or resinous wax (Delar), an instant set with the air-water syringe, little or no trimming, much lower cost; but they need a water bath, are brittle, and can get too thin for an MIP record. If you use VPS: don't cover the occluding surfaces of unprepared teeth (in MIP they are supposed to touch; material over the prep is fine), don't register soft tissue (it moves in the mouth but not in stone), and if missing teeth don't allow a stable mounting, use a record base. Two reasons a registration, whatever the material, rarely fits even when trimmed: the material's resilience, and detail greater than the stone cast's. Occlusion is measured in microns; 20 µm off and the crown is out of occlusion. Used with care, VPS can be very accurate; otherwise it adds error. Trim windows so you can see the cusps seat. Five requirements of interocclusal records (Dawson): 1. the record must not move teeth or displace soft tissue; 2. its accuracy must be verifiable in the mouth; 3. it must fit the casts as accurately as it fits the mouth; 4. its accuracy must be verifiable on the casts; 5. it must not distort in storage or transport to the lab. Eccentric records and programming the articulator Eccentric records program the articulator to follow the patient's condylar movement. They are most meaningful when mounted in CR (bilateral balanced occlusion in dentures, reorganized treatment). The protrusive record: the mandible moves forward from CR 3-5 mm, without lateral deviation; one record sets the SCI on both sides. Lateral records: the mandible moves in laterotrusion 3-5 mm; you need two (left and right working motion), and each sets the contralateral SCI and the contralateral medial-wall settings (Bennett angle and immediate side shift): a right lateral record sets the left side. Protrusive records are preferred. The SCI measured with a lateral record (down the medial wall) is steeper than the SCI from a protrusive record (down the articular eminence). If the goal is posterior disclusion, contacts that are avoided in protrusion will also miss in right and left laterotrusion, so the shallower protrusive SCI is the safer setting: if the articulator is shallower than the patient, the patient just gets more disclusion; if it is steeper, the restoration may hit. For the same reason many clinicians set an arbitrary 30°: most patients' protrusive angles range from about 20 to 60° (commonly 35-40°), so a 30° setting gives decent anatomy and still discludes in the mouth (20° makes the cusps too shallow). For a bilateral balanced denture you would do the opposite; that comes later. Why 3-5 mm? Beyond that the condyle's path is curving and the teeth are separated anyway. The orbiting condyle's path curves, so the Bennett angle measured depends on where the record is taken: at 3-5 mm of condylar movement the angle is larger; at 7-10 mm it is smaller, which builds narrower fossae on the posterior teeth and more likely interferences. To program: release the centric latch and loosen the settings (both SCIs for a protrusive record; the contralateral SCI and the Bennett and side-shift settings for a lateral); seat the record on the upper cast and the lower cast into it; the condylar element now touches neither the superior fossa nor the medial wall; adjust the SCI until the element touches the superior fossa surface, then tighten (a protrusive record is done here); for a lateral record, adjust the Bennett angle and/or immediate side shift until the medial wall touches the element, tighten, and repeat with the other side's record. Semi-adjustable articulators adapt to patient-specific condylar movement, a significant advantage over non-adjustable ones. They take more time, "but well worth the effort," because they minimize intraoral adjustment, and they cost more. Some models (including the Denar 320, calibrated) are interchangeable: mounted casts move between articulators without losing accuracy, so the articulator doesn't travel to the lab (Oral Arts keeps calibrated Denar 320s), fewer articulators are needed and less damage happens. As a resident, before interchangeability, he used 17 articulators to run his cases. Fully adjustable articulators The most sophisticated instruments in dentistry for reproducing mandibular movement, with precise adjustments for the condylar inclination (lateral and protrusive paths separately, not just sagittal), the Bennett angle and immediate lateral shift (curved or custom paths, not straight), the rotating condyle (its small superior-inferior and anterior-posterior motion affects cusp height and fossa depth on the working side) and the intercondylar distance (not everyone is 4 inches; it changes the eccentric paths of opposing cusps, so the groove and ridge positions). The Denar D5A is one; the Denar 330 is a semi-adjustable that comes close. Programming them takes complex procedures: 1. the exact hinge axis with a kinematic facebow (a hinge-axis locator: the upper bow holds a grid, the lower a stylus; hinge the mandible in CR and adjust the stylus until it only rotates; the point was once tattooed on the skin); 2. dynamic capture of mandibular movement, because positional records can't show it: the pantograph captures the "timing" of movement, with a lower bow carrying 6 recording tables and an upper bow 6 styli, the teeth separated by a central bearing device so they can't influence the motion, through protrusive and right and left laterotrusive movements, then transferred to the articulator and adjusted until it reproduces the tracings (hours of work); 3. a CR record. Today's jaw-tracking systems (SAM Axioquick, ModJaw 4D, Whip Mix Cadiax, KaVo Protar, the 3Shape Trios's patient-specific motion) capture the same thing in minutes and feed a virtual articulator. Any record is influenced by the patient knowing it is being taken, so practice and relaxation help. Record thickness. On a fully adjustable articulator the exact hinge axis is captured, so the arc of opening and closing in terminal hinge movement is the same on the patient and the articulator, and the thickness of the CR record doesn't affect accuracy. On a semi-adjustable articulator the arbitrary facebow gives an AHA that only estimates the PHA, so the arcs differ and the thicker the record, the more error. So on a semi-adjustable: make CR records with minimal thickness, or at the vertical dimension you intend to treat, where the two arcs meet and the articulator is "dead on." The major advantage of a fully adjustable articulator is duplicating the patient, in the hope of minimal intraoral adjustment. The disadvantages: time-consuming, technique-sensitive instrumentation and significant expense. In the analog world that hope rarely came true; digital workflows are making the concept a reality. Selecting an articulator 1. The patient's occlusion. Anterior guidance usually predominates in eccentric tooth contact, because it is closer to the teeth. With strong anterior guidance, a less sophisticated articulator can be used for posterior teeth (a crown on #20 will disclude). With poor anterior guidance (little vertical or horizontal overlap, malaligned or missing teeth, pathology; skeletal Class II arch discrepancies, edge-to-edge Class III), the posterior determinant controls more of the movement and a more sophisticated articulator is needed. It is hard to justify a non-adjustable articulator for any tooth that is part of the anterior guidance. 2. The extent of the restorative work. The more the articulator mimics the patient, the less intraoral adjustment. Minor procedures can use simpler instruments; complex reconstruction (a four-unit bridge from #22 to #18 replaces half the posterior occlusion) needs more sophisticated ones. "The job dictates the tool, not the other way around." 3. The limits of the articulator system, in how much intraoral adjustment will be needed. 4. The skill of the clinician: "A semi-adjustable articulator in the hands of a knowledgeable clinician may be of greater assistance in treatment than a fully adjustable articulator in the hands of an inexperienced operator" (add to that, a careless one), and if the records are careless or the casts inaccurately mounted, any articulator loses its usefulness. His selection table, in short: a restoration discluded significantly by anterior guidance can go on any of the three; a restoration that is minimally discluded (eccentric interferences likely), part of the anterior guidance, one of several units, crossing the midline, with a change of VDO, a diagnostic CR mounting, steep or flat eminence, acute or flat curve of Spee, a steep occlusal plane or anatomic cusp height all call for at least a semi-adjustable (a fully adjustable does them best). The non-adjustable wins only on ease of lab use (expense) and ease of clinician use. "Anything that you can do in the laboratory that saves you clinic time is well worth the investment."
